posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: Of course it does!!! I apologize for not testing before writing! I just looked at my VB6 BLE code - plenty of comments in there :D, as the LWP3.0 just came out (2018, I believe) and there were some hub-firmware updates later. That was all so exciting back then - here on EB a real "decoding-the-protocol-frenzy" was raging, as you may recall ... Anyway, before BLE, all my trains were RCX (+433 MHz RF), PF (+433 MHz RF) or RC (+433 MHz RF) operated through a first generation of MulPI. An Arduino Mega was in charge of that. Then PoweredUp came out, and I added BLE to my VB6 Train Control program (after /n software gave me their BLE stack for VB6 for free :D). But my Sinclair ZX Spectrum did not have BLE - so MulPI got an ESP32 upgrade ... Anyway, my own comments told me that all services etc. are the same and a Technic hub connects in the same way a City hub does ... And it works!!! There were some things, in the console (it did not know the hub type, and the (PUp LED) ID was unknown to LEGO Blockly. But then it fixed everything by itself - and knows that a two-port hub is called a "City hub". How is this even possible??? You are a genius, Yves! This is what the Status window says: [10:17:30] Connected: Remote1 [10:18:04] Connected: City1 [10:18:04] City1: Check Console log for new Device info. The PUp remote also connects nicely(!) and works flawlessly. In this case most LPF2 blocks don't apply of course, as the remote has no sensors nor outputs (apart from the LED). Wow. Thanks a million again!!! All the best, Thorsten

posts.title: [MOC] Mechatech 6x6 All Terrain Tow Truck (42070 10th Year Anniversary Model)
posts.text: And i forgot to, post these pictures. Here is the model with bullbar removed:). Here is shot for the rear axle suspension:). The rear axles uses linkages when other axle is up the other axle goes down. This is my first moc which uses this and this helps with the balance:). Behind the scenes stuff:). Developement pictures:). Ok, i normally dont use old and retired pieces. But this model is my first which uses old and retired pieces. The turntable is from 42006 and this model is not compatible with the new and current 2015 Arocs turntable design. When i started this project my vision was to control 4 functions with 2 gearboxes. But i soon runned out for availdable space. So i made only one gearbox which drives the 2 functions and all the other functions are operated separately. When i created the Mechatech Snow Cat i wasn't happy how the boom looked it was just too bulky and the connection to the chassis looked pretty rough. So i redesigned the boom from scratch for this model and luckily this boom doesn't look bulky. This model's outriggers are my most complex outriggers yet. If you are curious why in the instructions the test for the outriggers comes so late. Is because the side panes lock then so they won't detatch from the build during testing and if you have to adjust them it is pretty simple job. The front and rear outriggers operate at different speeds to make them operate synchronized. The drivetrain for the gearbox i designed pretty much firstly and it was always next to the engine and the shaft in display mode acts as an exchaust pipe and when you start playing with this model. You just connect the gear to the exchaust pipe and start playing:). The engine was firstly planned to be upright. But since the engine room did have little room i had to place the engine flat so it would fit:). And since this model is 1612 and really dense. This model is really heavy. But really strong. Since i do design my models with strict standards and durability in mind for rough playing:). This model the third model which uses my redesigned front axle for the unimog. Im really impressed how strong my designed front axle was and how reusable it was. This model probably is the heaviest which uses this type front axle:). I wish you to have a massive fun time building and playing with the Mechatech 6x6 All Terrain Tow Truck:).

posts.text: I don't sell my sets so there is no time pressure for me. It might take me years to complete some sets. I simply use Bricklink wanted lists, one for every set with missing pieces. I have quite a lot of incomplete sets and they are often buried in large containers under other plastic bags. So instead of putting the aquired missing pieces into the plastic bag for the set, I collect them in a separate "missing pieces" bag (not even sorted by set, just one large bag) and then update the "Have" count in the wanted list. When the wanted list is completed and I want to build the set, I pick the pieces from the bag, then I delete the wanted list.

posts.title: Orient Express-The Glacial Monarch
posts.text: Hello there! I am building a LEGO luxury train MOC (My Own Creation). It is based on nothing specific, but you can easily modify it. Along the way, I encountered a few building issues: 1. The Doors Most doors on LEGO trains use very simple, standard door parts. However, my luxury train has curved sides, so using normal LEGO or train doors would have ruined the look. I had to make custom doors with a curved bottom that fit flush with the train walls. At first, this went easily—I just used standard LEGO hinge pieces (2429/2430). But when they opened, they didn't look like real train doors. If you have ever seen a real luxury train door open, it basically pops out, slides, and sticks flat against the outside of the train. Throughout that entire opening process, you only ever see the outside of the door. With the simple hinge piece, the door swung wide open, exposing the back side of the door, which is inaccurate. I tried different techniques, but in the end, I used the method LEGO uses for their airplane doors. The piece I used is 30377 (the Battle Droid arm). However, when you attach it, it requires some open clearance space so the arm can swing out. This left a weird, empty hole in the train wall. To fix this, I added custom movable flaps to cover the gap. When the doors are closed, these flaps pivot flush with the rest of the train walls. When you want to open the doors, you just move the flap out of the way first. 2. The Bogies (Wheel Assemblies) Another issue was choosing whether the train should have shared bogies (Jacobs bogies) or separate, independent bogies per carriage. I ultimately decided to make them shared bogies because it gives the train a much cleaner, seamless look. Right now, I am currently working on a motorized version of the build, and I am also designing the train's locomotive."

posts.title: Bricklink Designer Program Trains Sets | 2024 & Beyond
posts.text: Are you using the PoweredUp (2-port) hub(s) and PUp L motors? If so, these run great when powered by the LEGO PF rechargeable LiPo #8878. That Lipo has an output voltage of 7.4V = 2 x 3.7V cells. In other words, you can use a much more powerful 2S high amperage LiPos, rather than 9V batteries. There is ample of space in your B-unit. Simply recharge the LiPo and the fun continues! 3 of my PUp operated trains have run on the #8878/#8809 combo for years now. But with that much space, I'd certainly use a non-LEGO 2S LiPo. Best Thorsten

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: @Bliss I just finished yesterday my build of the LEGO BDP #910066 Brick Railroad Locomotive (an FP7 in 8 wide). It is ready to go for two PUp Technic L motors (#88013) LEGO doesn't sell anymore (website says "out of stock" for a long time) along with the small white LEGO PUp hub (#88009) - which is still officially available. This hub has only two ports and no extra sensors inside. The locomotive runs fine on one L motor, just checked; I'll use the other output for a PUp LED. Is there any chance that you'll add this 2-port PUp hub to the LEGO Blockly list of devices it can connect to? If you need any info about UUIDs etc. I can pull them up, since four trains here run on PUp stuff. If not, I'll use an ESP32 as BLE server to connect the LEGO PUp remote and the hub, my usual approach. EDIT#1. EDIT#2 The LEGO PUp remote is of the type "bang-bang" when it connects directly to a hub, which is stupid. But when a PUp LED is attached, it does increase the speed step by step! It slowly comes back: Dumb PUp devices like the LED and the train motor do get the stepwise in/decrease feature when pressing +/-. Smarter devices like the PUp L motor just bang fully forward when pressing +, and bang fully reverse when pressing -. Now I remember, why my Crocodile needed an ESP ... But still, I would rather not use a cell phone or tablet at all. The ESP can then send the proper power settings with acceleration and deceleration profiles and speed control, which is nice for train operation. But it would be very pleasant to connect directly to the small hub with my laptop and use full range, carefully adjustable PWM blocks! Best Thorsten

posts.text: Hello it's again the time when i strike back with a new model:). After the successful launch of the Mechatech Mechadozer. Well it's Power Functions sucked. No Servo and open differentials. Plus the IR receiver was poorly placed so the reach from the remote was poor, plus the crane and bed looked really unfinished. Plus some other bits looked pretty rough and unfinished. So this was kind of a big task. How to resurrect and remake this hated model for its 10th anniversary and fixing its flaws:). So I started the huge task. For resurrecting and remaking this hated model. And finally here is the result. Here is the Mechatech 6x6 All Terrain Tow Truck, 42070 10th Anniversary Model:). This truck is beefy, bulky. Really utilitarian, backcountry, rough terrain, rugged looking:). Plus this is my first 6x6 All Terrain Vehicle:). And since the 42070 introduced the new dark azure color for the technic models. I decided that the Anniversary Model would do the same and the anniversary model uses the newish Reddish Orange color. For its special coloring, I think the Reddish Orange, Black and Yellow colorscheme looks really great:). Pls note. This model is not a 100% replica of the 42070. But a remake and a 10th anniversary model. The 42070 had a “ton” of “issues” so to create a remake and anniversary model I had pretty much a blank canvas to improve the 42070 for its anniversary model. But there are a few things which have to be in the remake and on the 10th anniversary model. The 6x6 drivetrain, the synchronized front and rear outriggers and the crane. Plus those critical functions are overhauled slightly for the remake to make them work better. So if you are a true die hard 42070 purist. This model isn't for you. Then this is a great companion to the 42070 and this will pair nicely to the 42070 on display. Plus since this is small and backed to the brim with functions. If you don't have space for the 42070 or you hate the 42070 because of its flaws this is a great alternative with the same functions and improved looks. Minus the electronics:). posts.title: Building Bellona: a 74-gun WIP
posts.text: Before I'd even tied the last knot in the rigging of my 80 gunner, I was already picking apart the design with faults and things to be improved. During the construction of that ship, I had acquired the superb book HMS Bellona, anatomy of the ship. I highly recommend this book for anyone looking to build a lego ship of the line, as it is packed with drawings and details covering from the keel to the crow's nest. This further highlighted how poorly shaped the 80 gunner was. Whilst I was preparing parts and ideas for the build, I received the marvellous Fortuna, which gave me a whole load of new ideas, and techniques, being a major source of inspiration. Due to the inspiration for the ship, and the preponderance of Bluecoat ships in my fleet, I decide this would be a Redcoat ship instead. My previous builds had been designed using Studio, but this time I instead drew out the waterline of the ship to scale, measured from the plans, and built from there instead. This is where the build currently stands, with the main deck almost complete, and the upper deck following along swiftly. I have been focusing on getting the masts up and rigged, leaving the bow and stern to the end. I went for the classic Nelson Chequer colours, which will contrast nicely against the fancy Bluecoat ships. As with the 80 gunner, this build is modular to ease transport. I used snot slopes for the main deck, whilst retaining hinges to form the tumblehome on the upper deck. The quarter galleries are roughly mocked up to give an idea of scale. The shaping around the underside of the stern is deceptively tricky, much worse than the bow, and is still quite blocky. Thankfully this area is down low and mostly in shadow, so this isn't too apparent. Everyone seems to like interiors, and despite my best efforts, the interior of the 80 gunner is basically inaccessible. Inspired by the Fortuna, the decks here come off in sections, although the areas around the masts and ends will be fixed. A cross section view. The ship breaks just ahead of the main mast, with the main deck being entirely filled with structure. The upper deck is quite similar to the 80 gunner. The bow is quite similar to the 80 gunner too, but I have now added some tumblehome here too. The stern chunk is further progressed at the moment, I need more decking to progress the bow half. Finally a view of the belly, showing all the structure that fills the main deck. I'm aiming to have this ship finished in time for the 2027 display season, so there's plenty of work to do. Let me know if there's anything you think I could improve, or needs changing.

To use an example of a precious project that I hope to earn some money from I’ve been developing an application, it’s taken me about 4-5 years because coding is not my area of expertise, despite the effort it’s taken me I plan to make the main functionality free and the additional albeit unnecessary features behind a paywall for a fairly low price as I’m thinking that over the long run the costs of maintenance for an offline app with no api’s will be minimal compared to what I’d earn from building a larger consumer base as a result of the free + paid enhancement model. TLDR I’m saying in the long run making your instructions and model more accessible will bring more sales than one pdf sold for £200.

posts.title: EMD diesel GP7 locomotive - New York Central two tone gray paint scheme - set 10133 style digital MOC (free LDD file)
posts.text: This model is my interpretation of the GP7 class of diesel locomotive (produced by EMD from 1949 to 1954) in New York Central colors. The model is also inspired by the 2004 LEGO set 10133 - Burlington Northern Santa Fe (BNSF) Locomotive, which is itself based on the much-later GP38-2 type. The GP7 and GP38-2 are similar in some respects, so I just had to backdate it into the earlier model of locomotive. This process necessitated the making of the high short hood as you see here, along with a few other changes to make the New York Central two-tone gray colors work. I did one accidental goof though - the long hood was technically the front on this road's engines, so right now the model is backwards! (With the way the short hood and cab are constructed, I'm not sure I can fix that...) The long hood of the loco. The letters 'NYC' go on the long hood, while under the cab go the engine's road number. The cab roof can be removed, with a seat for a single minifig and a control stand like in the original set 10133. This model is a proof of concept, and I won't be building it in the colors shown but it will be built very soon in a different two-color paint scheme. You'll just have to wait and see what that is, though! The free LDD file can be found on my Bricksafe page here. Thoughts?

posts.title: Lynx Kf41
posts.text: I am a commander of an actual Lynx KF41 in the Hungarian Defence Forces—a profession I truly love and enjoy. My hobby is building with LEGO. I’ve designed a LEGO version of the Lynx so that you, too, can experience what it’s like to work with this "big cat"! Here are some details about it. I’d love to hear your thoughts! 1:24 scale model. Dimensions: 34 cm long, 20 cm wide, and 20 cm high; weight: 1720 g; total parts: 2775. Features a 360-degree rotating turret and a separate 360-degree rotating commander’s cupola; both weapon barrels can be elevated and move in sync with their respective optics. Openable components include: the engine compartment, driver’s hatch, turret hatches, turret tool box, ammunition storage, Spike LR2 launcher container, troop compartment hatch, and the rear ramp. Detailed interior: driver’s station, engine compartment (with engine), turret, commander’s and gunner’s stations, and the troop compartment. The model can be motorized—an optional add-on consisting of 85+ additional parts, including an M-motor and a remote control. The tracks are powered independently, and the turret can be rotated via a motor. https://rebrickable.com/mocs/MOC-278955/Dgergo/lynx-kf41/#details
